chapter_theme: The last twenty poems of the Akananuru (Nittilakkovai 381 to 400), in the fixed order of lands: ten paalai poems of men gone for wealth and fame and of daughters gone with lovers, as heard by wives, friends and mothers; hill poems of night meetings, the diviner's rite and the pleading lover; mullai returns and invitations; a salt-girl met on the shore and a wedding chariot; and two Paranar courtesans who measure a lover's broken oath against the puram legends of Eyinan, Aththi and Vanji.

381.reading: Halfway across the wasteland the man tells his heart that she at home must be suffering more than they who crossed it: her body wasted like an enemy fort the Chera Vaanavan's army razed, sighing long, her eyes like a pair of blue water-lilies brimming with tears.
381.nuance: The road is built of killers (the yali tearing the elephant's tusk, the sun that has eaten the shade, the Vadukar with their dogs, the blood-bathed vultures that make the sky look like dusk), and the turn at line 13 (நம்மினும்) makes all of it a measure of her pain rather than his danger. Line 3 (குருகருந்தும்) and line 7 (கற்றுரிக் குடம்பை) are hard words in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the man parted from her, crossing the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: the vulture flock rising and reddening the sky

382.reading: With the lover listening outside at night, the friend tells the girl that their kin have resolved to hold the possession rite for Murugan, with kadamba tied, garlands, and many-voiced instruments, and that he, lord of the hill where a monkey floats down a waterfall on a jackfruit to the town's ford, must be told of it.
382.nuance: The opening maxim (others feel another's trouble; one's own trouble is one's own to bear) is aimed at the man: the rite would publish a sickness that is his doing, and the friend sends the news to him so that he will act. The monkey riding the jackfruit down to the big town's ford can be read as a hidden image of the girl carried into public talk, but no second correspondence is anchored, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the monkey, the jackfruit and Murugan's rite of the hills

383.reading: The mother whose daughter has run off with a youth speaks to the vayalai creeper the girl watered every day and stripped for her leaf-skirt: the girl who never thought of the mother who raised her has crossed many lands with him amid the town's gossip, and now no one will water the withering creeper.
383.nuance: The mother cannot address the girl, so she addresses the plant, and its needs become an inventory of the daughter's lost daily life: the full water-pot, the jumping bangles, the ringing anklets, the glance at her mother's face as she came back. Line 5 suggests the creeper's leaves were also sought for the youth's garland.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has eloped across the wasteland

384.reading: Home from the king's campaign, the man asks his charioteer whether he yoked the wind or his own mind as horses, since he knew only that he mounted the chariot and then heard 'get down' at his wife's house in the mullai woodland; then he embraces him, takes him in, and the wife receives a guest.
384.nuance: The return is told as a lapse of time: longing has abolished the road. The last line turns the charioteer into the household's first guest, so the reunion is completed as hospitality.

thinai_evidence.note: the mullai woodland, its millet village and its hares

comparisons.tenor: the charioteer's mind as the horses

385.reading: The foster mother grieves that the girl, who said nothing while her playmates and mothers prepared a festival in their house rich as the Chola's Uranthai, has gone off with her lover, swinging joyfully on a banyan's root in the wasteland as he pushes her, and that she should shed her anklets for him and go to an unknown land is cruel.
385.nuance: The swing scene is imagined, and imagined as happiness: the cruelty the foster mother names is not the girl's danger but her forgetting. The anklet removal (சிலம்பு கழீஇ) belongs to the wedding at home; the girl performs it, in the mother's mind, for the youth on the road. How lines 6 to 7 and 17 attach is not certain in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter has left with her lover

comparisons.tenor: her hair tossing as she swings

386.reading: The woman tells the husband, lord of a town where the otter hunts vaalai fish each day, that she felt the shame Kanaiyan felt when Paanan broke the Aariya wrestler, when his mistress came in secret by day, called herself a neighbour and a younger sister, stroked her brow and hair, and left.
386.nuance: The shame is double: she was flattered and touched by the rival who now has her husband, and she recognised the trick only after. The comparison to Kanaiyan's shame is a public one: a patron watching his champion fall in the ring. The otter's daily hunt for fresh fish is the husband's appetite.

colophon.thurai: தோழி வாயின் மறத்தது. தலைமகள் தகுதி சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the pond, the otter and the vaalai fish of the farm town

ullurai.tenor: the husband and the women he seeks

pairs.situation: the husband who comes home tainted
he seeks a fresh woman day after day

ullurai.speaker_fit: the wife (or the friend) uses an otter of the town's own pond in a marutham poem (porul 7.26, 7.27)

387.reading: The friend tells the man leaving while his wife's jewels slip and her eyes weep to say, if he can, that he will come back, for the forest he goes to is one where a quail hen, frightened by the hunters' call, cries to her mate, and where at a lizard's small cry among the hero-stones even lords with elephants halt and turn back.
387.nuance: மன்னோ makes the request ironic: on a road ruled by omens no traveller can promise a return. Lines 4 to 8 (the washerwoman's starched cloth) seem to describe the quail's striped markings, but our text does not settle the construction, and the last line is obscure.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகளது குறிப்பறிந்து தோழி தலைமகனைச் செலவபங்கச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man is about to leave across the forest

iraicchi.act: the quail hen, frightened by the hunters' decoy call, calls her mate to her
iraicchi.sense: even the hen in danger calls her mate close, so the wife, afraid, needs the man beside her and he should not go

388.reading: The girl tells her friend, with the lover listening, how a young hunter with a hound came to their millet platform asking whether a wounded tusker had passed, and how, aching for him, she is now held by the mother's diviner, who says his god caused the sickness; she would ask the velan whether his god goes hunting with a bloodied arrow on a deer's track.
388.nuance: The question is a joke with a point: the 'god' who seized her is the hunter, and asking it would tell the truth to the household without a confession. The hunter's pretext (a wounded elephant) is the usual opening of the day meeting.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறிச் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தலைமகள் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது. தோழ தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியதுமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: guarding millet from a platform in the vengai, and Murugan's diviner

389.reading: The wife tells her friend that the man who once dressed her hair, painted her brow and breasts and shoulders, reddened her feet and would not leave her bed even by day has gone, to fill beggars' hands, silence his scorners and fix his fame, beyond the Chera Vaanavaramban's land into summer forest where a tiger that has killed a tusker roars like thunder.
389.nuance: She gives his reasons in her own voice, and they are the puram virtues (giving, honour, fame); the complaint is that those virtues are what took him. The adornments she lists are acts of his hands, so the memory is of being cared for, not only of being loved.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் வற்புறுக்குந் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has left her to seek wealth

occasion.words: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட தலைமகள் வற்புறுக்குந் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது

390.reading: The man tells his companion, or his heart, that his heart is lost to a salt-trader's girl who went from street to street calling 'paddy for salt, measure for measure', who, when he blocked her way and joked that he could not price the salt of her body, looked at him angrily, asked who he was to stop her, and walked off smiling.
390.nuance: The opening question (is the salt-carriers' wandering life a good one, then?) is the lover's envy of the people she belongs to. Her look is war and her smile is release, in one movement; the joke about the salt 'living in your body' is a flirtation she rebuffs and enjoys.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் பாங்கற்குச் சொல்லியது; நெஞ்சிற்குச் சொல்லிய தூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: salt from the brine pans and the salt-traders

391.reading: The wife tells her friend that each time she sees the tuft of hair her lover dressed with athiral flowers the sellers could not sell and with mullai, she remembers the old adornment; even if he returns in a few days her eyes will not sleep, for he crossed summer wasteland where an elephant's limp trunk looks like a snake entering a hill.
391.nuance: The flowers he chose were the cheap ones the hawkers threw away, which makes the memory more intimate, not less. The elephant too weak to lift its tusks is the hot land's exhaustion, set against the care she remembers.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover has crossed the wasteland away from her

392.reading: The friend, having agreed to help the pleading lover, asks the girl to consent: his wasted body is like a tusker's that has lost its mate and refuses fodder, it would hurt to send him away ruined, and the lord of that roaring hill will hardly leave her; if he ever did, she herself would stand fast like Nannan and restore her beauty.
392.nuance: The night scene (a sling's crack scattering millet-raiding elephants, the tiger's roar, the jungle fowl's cry, the peacock dancing, the whole mountain afraid) shows a land in which one sound sets everything moving, as the friend hopes her word will. The story of Nannan holding his spear against a besieging king is told too briefly to be sure of.

colophon.thurai: பின்னின்ற தலைமகற்குக் குறைநேர்ந்த தோழி தலைமகட்குக் குறைநயப்பக் கூறியது.

thinai_evidence.note: millet fields, elephants and tigers of the hills

comparisons.vehicle: வீழ்பிடி கெடுத்த வெண்கோட்டு யானை உண்குளகு மறுத்த உயக்கத்

comparisons.tenor: the friend's resolve to restore the girl

393.reading: The friend tells the wife that though he has gone beyond Venkadam, past the land of Pulli where herders cook varagu millet and share it with milk among hungry travellers, he will not stay long, having forgotten the sweet sleep of her hair washed with thagaram and dressed with blue lily and athiral.
393.nuance: Most of the poem is the herders' cooking, told step by step (threshing on the rock, pounding, boiling in a stone hearth), and its point is that travellers on that road are fed: the comfort is that he is safe there. The closing memory of her dressed hair answers 391, where the wife looks at the same flowers.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone far on a journey for work

394.reading: Having brought the girl to the night meeting, the friend invites the lover, lord of great gifts, to come one day to their little home in the poor-soil village where a hare hides at the goatherd's whistle, and, after his young men have eaten termite-rice with curd and butter, to eat milk rice that his wife prepares there.
394.nuance: Line 1 is a pun: களவும் புளித்தன says the karanda fruit has soured, and also that the secret love has gone sour. 'Your wife' (நின் மனையோள்) names the girl as what she would be once married, so the invitation to a meal is a demand for marriage.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறித் தலைமகளை இடத்துய்த்து வந்து தோழி தலைமகனை வரைவு கடாஅயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the goatherd, millet and hare of the scrub

comparisons.tenor: the red doorway of the little house

395.reading: The wife tells her friend it would be good if he came back now to end the tears of eyes like rain-filled blue lilies, he who crossed the bamboo hills of dry forest where a stag, chasing a mirage and lost off the path, calls its grazing doe in a broken voice that travellers mistake for a man's.
395.nuance: The stag that ran after a mirage and lost its mate is set on his road: it is an image of what that land does to partners, and of the cry he will hear there.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has crossed the wasteland, leaving her

iraicchi.act: the stag, separated from its doe while chasing a mirage, calls to her in a broken voice
iraicchi.sense: the man on that road will hear a parted creature crying for its mate and so feel his own parting and come back

396.reading: The courtesan holds her lover and will not let him go: Aay Eyinan died fighting Minjili at Paazhi to keep his word to those Nannan drove out, but he, after swearing before the god and taking her wrist, has become another's; she fears his wife will snatch him as the Kaviri snatched Aththi from Manthi, so he must give back her beauty, splendid as the Chera's Vanji, before he goes.
396.nuance: Each legend is chosen against him: Eyinan kept a promise of refuge with his life, the river's seizing of Aththi stands for the wife's claim, and Vanji, seat of the king who carved his bow on the northern mountain, prices the beauty he owes her. Line 10 (மார்புதரு கல்லாய்) can also be read as 'you who never learned to give your chest'.

thinai_evidence.note: the courtesan's quarrel with a married man

comparisons.tenor: the lover who broke his oath
the wife taking the man away

397.reading: The foster mother says the hasty youth, instead of taking her daughter in marriage at their festive house, decided the cloudless wasteland would be easy for the girl and led her off before the cool season, through forest where a kite perches on a yaa tree, taking the red gash an elephant tore in an omai trunk for flesh.
397.nuance: Her grief is set against the wedding that should have been: the house where the drum never dries is named so that the elopement reads as a festival refused. The kite's mistake (red bark for meat) is the land's hunger. Line 2 is hard to construe in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the youth has led the girl away across the wasteland

comparisons.tenor: the red wound in the omai's bark

398.reading: Wasting with longing, the girl speaks to the flooding stream from her lover's hill: she reproaches it for slipping away ashamed under his hill's flowers instead of telling him of her pallor and tears, and asks what harm there would be if it rested a while in her father's flowering forest, before going back to the country where a spent elephant groans as it embraces its tired mate.
398.nuance: The stream is a messenger from his hill that she blames for his silence, and she offers it the hospitality she cannot offer him. The elephant that, wounded and spent, still holds its mate is the care his land knows and he withholds. Several lines (9 to 16) are hard to construe.

colophon.thurai: காமமிக்க கழிபடர் கிளவியால் (விரைவிடத்துக்கண்) தலைமகள் தலைமகன் வரையினின்றும் போந்த ஆற்றொடு புலந்து சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill country, its vengai and elephants

iraicchi.act: the elephant, spent and wounded from fighting a tiger, still embraces its tired mate
iraicchi.sense: even the elephants of his hill hold their mates in distress, yet their lord leaves her to waste

399.reading: The friend tells the wife, whose hair smells like the Himalayan forest, that her husband will not stay away without coming back to embrace her as if drinking her in, though he crossed sun-scorched hills where a doe, chewing nelli fruit, listens to the lonely notes of herders' bamboo flutes as they rest their cattle in konrai shade.
399.nuance: The herders' flute is called lonely (புலம்புகொள்) and the doe listens to it: the road he is on is full of sounds of solitude that will turn him home.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband is away across the hills

400.reading: After the wedding the friend tells the bride it is laughable now that they once feared gossip even if she ran off with him: the day the lord of the shore came, his strong chariot racing over milk-white sand and mud like water down a ford, their old town of palmyras by the roaring sea looked new, the neythal buds opening and smelling of new toddy.
400.nuance: The chariot passage is the same apparatus akam uses for the lover's secret night visits, here driven openly to the wedding, so speed now means eagerness rather than stealth. The town that gossiped (அழுங்கல் ஊர்) is the town that looks new.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் வரைந் தெய்திய பின்றைத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove, the neythal flower and the palmyras

occasion.words: தலைமகன் வரைந் தெய்திய பின்றைத் தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லியது

links.note: Both are the plea of the one left behind against a departure: the couplet says tell your quick return to those still alive; 387 asks him to say he will return, and then shows a road where great men turn back at a lizard's cry.
links.teaches: The couplet only doubts the traveller's promise; the poem shows why it is empty, since on that road a return depends on omens and beasts, not on the man's word.

links.note: Both are the man's account of a first sight, and both set a simple girl (பேதை) against eyes that make war (அமர்த்தன / அமர்த்தனள்).
links.teaches: The couplet's paradox of war-making eyes in an artless girl gets a cause in the poem: she glares because a stranger blocks her road and jokes about her body, so the 'deadly' look is her self-possession, and it ends in a smile.

links.note: Both speak of a lover who took a woman's beauty in exchange: the couplet's woman says he took grace and modesty and gave sickness and pallor; the courtesan of 396 demands her beauty back before he goes.
links.teaches: Read together they show the claim that a lover owes back the beauty he took was not the wife's alone: the courtesan states it as a debt to be repaid, which the couplet's wife can only lament.

links.note: Both are Paranar's courtesan poems, both end with the demand to give back her beauty and then go (நலம்தந்து சென்மே), and both use the Kaviri carrying off Aththi.
links.teaches: In 376 the river's seizing of Aththi is left without its tenor; 396 names it (I fear your wife will take you as the Kaviri hid Aththi), so the legend served Paranar as a fixed figure for the wife's lawful claim over the courtesan.

links.note: 208 tells how Aay Eyinan fell to Minjili at Paazhi and the birds shaded him; 396 says he died because he had promised 'fear not' to those Nannan drove from Punnadu.
links.teaches: 396 supplies the cause behind 208's famous death: Eyinan died keeping a promise of refuge, which is why a courtesan could cite him against a lover who broke an oath made before a god.

links.note: Kanaiyan appears in 44 as the chief captured by the Chola after Pazhaiyan fell, and in 386 as the patron shamed when Paanan broke his Aariya wrestler.
links.teaches: The akam poets used Kanaiyan only in defeat, once in capture and once in public shame, so his name had become a byword for humiliation before an onlooking crowd, which is exactly what the wife of 386 feels.

links.note: Puram 2 praises the Chera as வான வரம்பன், whose realm runs from the sea of sunrise to the sea of sunset; in 389 the husband goes beyond Vaana varamban's good land into tiger country.
links.teaches: The title that in puram means a king bounded only by the sky becomes in akam the edge of the safe world: the lover's journey is measured as going past a realm that claims to have no beyond.

links.note: Both are Mamoolanar's comfort poems: the man has gone beyond Pulli's good land (புல்லி நன்னாட்டு உம்பர்), where herders feed travellers, and he will not delay (நீடலர்).
links.teaches: Together they show a fixed comforting formula in which the herders' hospitality on Pulli's road is the reason the friend gives for the man's safety, so the same road scene doubles as evidence that he will come back.

links.note: In 391 the wife sees the tuft he dressed with athiral and mullai and remembers; in 393 the friend says he cannot stay away, having forgotten the sleep beside her hair dressed with blue lily and summer athiral.
links.teaches: The athiral in her hair is the shared token of the separation: for the wife it is proof of loss, while the friend turns the same token into proof that he must return.

links.note: Both are hill poems spoken at the night meeting with the lover listening, and both turn on the household's possession rite for Murugan.
links.teaches: The rite works two ways in the kurinji poems: in 382 its threat is news to hurry the lover, while in 388 the girl plans to use the diviner's own diagnosis to name the hunter, so the rite becomes the channel through which secret love is disclosed.

links.note: 394 invites the lover to eat milk rice in a mullai village home 'as your wife prepares it'; 384 shows the returned husband bringing a guest into such a home, where the wife receives him.
links.teaches: The friend's invitation in 394 pictures, as a reason to marry, the very scene 384 shows as marriage achieved: a mullai home where the wife serves guests.

links.note: Both foster mothers set the girl's flight against a festival at home: in 385 a festival is prepared and the girl says nothing; in 397 the youth will not take her in marriage at the house where the drum never dries.
links.teaches: Read together they show the elopement grieved as a refused home wedding, blamed in one poem on the girl's silence and in the other on the youth's haste.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage: the formal union that ends secret love, sought or pressed for in the akam poems
new_concepts.label_source: the colophon of 394 (வரைவு கடாஅயது) and of 400 (வரைந் தெய்திய)

new_concepts.gloss: the appointed meeting place and time of secret lovers, by day (பகற்குறி) or by night (இரவுக்குறி)
the diviner of Murugu, whom the mother calls when she reads the girl's lovesickness as possession
the velan's rite of possession by Murugu, and the ground where it is performed
new_concepts.label_source: the verse's word (Akananuru 388, line 18: வெறியென); 382 lines 3 to 7 describe the rite (அணங்கயர் வியன் களம்)

source_issues: 382: the colophon thurai reads தலைமகட்கச், a misprint for தலைமகட்குச்.
384: line 4 reads அறிந்தன்றொ இலெனே, apparently for அறிந்தன்றோ இலெனே.
386: the colophon thurai reads வாயின் மறத்தது, a misprint for வாயில் மறுத்தது.
387: the colophon thurai reads செலவபங்கச், a misprint for செலவழுங்கச்.
388: the colophon's second alternative reads தோழ தலைமகட்குச், a misprint for தோழி.
398: the colophon thurai carries a bracketed phrase (விரைவிடத்துக்கண்), apparently an editor's insertion.
400: lines 15 and 16 read பால்கண்ட டன்ன and கால்கண்ட டன்ன with a doubled ட, apparently for பால்கண்டன்ன and கால்கண்டன்ன.
